note: Ifera Hurmiz, mother of King Shapur of Persia, sent four hundred dinars to Rabbi Ami, who refused them, and then to Rava, who accepted them to keep peace with the kingdom. Rabbi Ami was angry. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Ami thought Rava should have given the money to poor gentiles rather than poor Jews, and in fact Rava had done just that. Rabbi Ami was angry only because the people who told him the story had not told it to the end.
why: The Sages have been debating whether charity given by non-Jewish nations earns them merit. This incident shows two Sages facing the question in practice, when a Persian queen sends a gift.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who refused the queen's gift and was angry that Rava accepted it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who accepted the gift to keep peace with the kingdom and gave it to poor gentiles.

terms.meaning: A person who is not Jewish.
Keeping good relations with the ruling power, here the Persian king's court.

flag: The STORY segments hold only the Gemara's follow-up explanation; the incident itself (the queen's gift, Rabbi Ami's refusal, Rava's acceptance) is in the BEFORE segment just preceding.

note: Two people each claimed a piece of land had belonged to their ancestors. The first brought witnesses that it had been his ancestors' and that he had worked it for the years needed to establish ownership; the second brought witnesses only that he had worked it for those years. Rav Naḥman ruled that the two testimonies about working the land cancel each other out, leaving the testimony about the ancestors, so the land stays with the first man. Rava objected that the first man's witnesses had been contradicted. Rav Naḥman answered that they were contradicted only about working the land, not about whose ancestors owned it.
why: The Gemara next asks whether Rav Naḥman and Rava are repeating an older dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda: whether witnesses contradicted by other witnesses may still be believed.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Judge who awarded the land to the man whose ancestors' ownership went unchallenged.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who objected that contradicted witnesses cannot be relied on.

terms.meaning: If someone openly works land and eats its produce for the required number of years without protest, the court presumes he owns it.

note: A man challenged another's hold on a field: what do you want with this land? The holder said he had bought it from him and showed a bill of sale. The first man said the bill was forged. The holder leaned over and whispered to Rabba: yes, it is forged, but I had a real bill that was lost, so I kept this one in hand for whatever it was worth. Rabba reasoned that the man had no reason to lie, since he could simply have claimed the bill was genuine. Rav Yosef objected: what are you relying on, this bill? An admitted forgery is just a worthless shard.
why: Rav Idi bar Avin rules right after this that in land cases the law follows Rabba, so the land stays with the man holding it. A matching case about a forged loan note follows, where the law goes the other way.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Judge who believed the holder, since he could have lied more easily.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who objected that a forged bill proves nothing.

terms.meaning: A written deed, signed by witnesses, recording the purchase of land.

note: A man demanded a hundred dinars from another and showed a promissory note. The other said the note was forged. The lender leaned over and whispered to Rava: yes, it is forged, but I had a real note that was lost, so I kept this one in hand for whatever it was worth. Rabba reasoned that the man had no reason to lie, since he could simply have claimed the note was genuine. Rav Yosef objected that an admitted forgery is just a worthless shard and cannot be relied on.
why: It mirrors the forged bill of sale case just before. Rav Idi bar Avin then rules that with money the law follows Rav Yosef, so the money stays with the alleged borrower, unlike the land case.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge to whom the lender whispered his admission.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sage who reasoned the lender had no reason to lie.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who objected that a forged note proves nothing.

terms.meaning: A written document recording a loan, which the lender can use to collect the debt in court.

flag: The man whispers to Rava but Rabba answers; in the matching case just before it is Rabba throughout, so the name may be a scribal variant.

note: Abaye offered to show Rava how the swindlers of Pumbedita operate. An owner asks a craftsman for his cloak back, and the craftsman says it never happened. The owner says he has witnesses who saw it with him; the craftsman says that was a different cloak. The owner says: bring it out and let us look. The craftsman says: I will not bring it out. Rava answered that the craftsman's claim holds, because the teaching on this speaks of an owner who saw his own cloak there.
why: The Gemara is discussing items left with craftsmen and when an owner can reclaim them. Rava reads the earlier teaching as requiring that the owner actually saw his item; Rav Ashi then shows how a clever owner can meet that test.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who describes the trick of the swindlers of Pumbedita.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who holds that the craftsman's claim is valid.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

note: After the Second Temple was destroyed, many Jews stopped eating meat and drinking wine, because both had been offered on the altar, which was gone. Rabbi Yehoshua asked: then should we not eat bread, since the meal-offerings have ceased? They said they could live on other produce. Nor fruit, since the first fruits have ceased? Other fruit, they said. Nor water, since the water libation has ceased? They fell silent. He told them: not to mourn at all is impossible, but to mourn too much is also impossible, since the Sages impose only what most people can bear. Instead, plaster your house but leave a small patch bare; prepare a meal but leave out a small item; a woman may adorn herself but leave out one small thing.
why: The discussion has just taught that one may not fully plaster a house, as mourning for the Temple. This teaching shows where that limited practice comes from: Rabbi Yehoshua's answer to people who wanted to mourn far more.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Sage who argued with the ascetics and set limits on mourning.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who said the bare patch should be one cubit by one cubit.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sage who said the bare patch should face the entrance.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who said the item left out of a meal is like small fried fish.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who said a woman leaves some hair at her temple unremoved.

terms.meaning: People who deny themselves ordinary pleasures; here, those who gave up meat and wine in mourning.
Offerings of flour brought on the Temple altar.
The first ripe produce, which farmers brought to the Temple.
Water poured on the Temple altar as an offering.

note: Rabbi Yehuda told of a man in Tzalmon who planted his vineyard with rows sixteen cubits apart. He bent the branches of each pair of rows to one side and sowed the cleared ground, switching sides the next year. The case came before the Sages and they permitted it. Rav Yosef answered that he did not know about this, but recalled a case in a village of shepherds: Rav Yehuda told a man who had sold trees to give the buyer enough land for an ox and its gear. Rav Yosef did not know how much that was until he learned that a tree must be planted four cubits from a neighbor's field, to leave room for work, and concluded that it meant four cubits.
why: The Gemara is asking how far apart trees may stand and still count as one unit, so the buyer gets the land under them. Abaye cites the Tzalmon case for the sixteen-cubit view; Rav Yosef answers with Rav Yehuda's ruling to back his smaller figure.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage who reports the Tzalmon vineyard case.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who answers with a case he witnessed and works out its meaning.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Judge who told the seller to give enough land for an ox and its gear.

terms.meaning: An ancient measure of length, roughly the length of a forearm.
A teaching from the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

flag: Two separate incidents are joined: the Tzalmon vineyard (cited by Abaye) and Rav Yehuda's ruling in the village of shepherds (cited by Rav Yosef against him).

note: Issur, a convert, had twelve thousand dinars deposited with Rava. His son Rav Mari was conceived before Issur converted but born after, and was away at a study hall when Issur lay dying. Rava reasoned that Rav Mari had no way to get the money: not by inheritance, since such a son does not inherit; not as a deathbed gift, which follows inheritance rules; and not by any formal act of acquisition, since the coins were not with Issur, he had no land, and Rava would not come if sent for. Rav Ika, son of Rav Ami, asked why Issur could not admit the money was Rav Mari's. Meanwhile a written admission came out of Issur's house. Rava was angry: they are teaching people claims and causing me a loss.
why: The Sages have asked whether a dying man's admission that he owes money counts as valid. The Gemara brings this incident as proof that it does: Issur's written admission secured the money for his son.

people.name: Issur the convert
people.about: A convert who had money deposited with Rava and lay dying.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: Issur's son, conceived before his father converted and born after.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage holding Issur's money, who expected to keep it.

people.name: Rav Ika, son of Rav Ami
people.about: Sage who pointed out that Issur could simply admit the money was his son's.

terms.meaning: A person who has formally joined the Jewish people.

terms.term: gift of a person on his deathbed
terms.meaning: The Sages let a dying person give property away by word alone, but such a gift follows the rules of inheritance.
A formal act, such as handing over an object, that transfers ownership; it does not work for coins.

note: In Bnei Brak a man sold part of the property he had inherited from his father, and then died. His relatives challenged the sale, saying he had still been a minor when he died. They asked Rabbi Akiva whether they might examine the body. He said they were not permitted to disgrace him, and besides, the signs of puberty tend to change after death.
why: The Sages disagree whether an heir may sell his father's property at eighteen or only at twenty. Rabbi Zeira cites this case against the view of twenty: a twenty-year-old counts as an adult anyway, so examining the body would prove nothing.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Sage who forbade examining the dead man's body.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Sage who cites the case to challenge one view of the age of sale.

terms.meaning: Someone who has not reached legal adulthood; his sale of inherited land is not valid.
Physical signs, such as body hair, by which Jewish law marks a young man as an adult.
